title: Sign-OPT: A Query-Efficient Hard-label Adversarial Attack
authors: Minhao Cheng, Simranjit Singh, Patrick Chen, Pin-Yu Chen, Sijia Liu, Cho-Jui Hsieh

pages.title: You only need the sign
pages.subtitle: The Sign-OPT idea in one sentence

blocks.html: OPT turned the hard-label attack into a real optimization problem, but it left an expensive bill: every gradient step required estimating the boundary distance $g(\theta)$ by a full binary search, and you needed many such estimates per step. Sign-OPT's insight is almost embarrassingly simple in hindsight. To decide which way to step, you do not need the precise value of the directional derivative — you only need its sign: did this nudge bring the boundary closer or push it farther? And that sign can be read from a single hard-label query.

An analogy: imagine descending a hill in fog. OPT carefully surveys the exact elevation in each candidate direction before deciding — slow and overkill. Sign-OPT just feels with one foot whether each direction tilts down or up, and walks toward the down votes. You lose the magnitude, but for choosing a direction the sign is all you ever needed.
To take a good descent step you do not need the value of the directional derivative — only its sign, obtainable with one extra query per probe direction.

pages.title: Same hard-label setting, same scoreboard
pages.subtitle: What we are optimizing, and what counts as winning

blocks.html: Sign-OPT lives in the same world as the rest of this family. In the hard-label / decision-based threat model the attacker may feed the model any input and observes only the final predicted label — no probabilities, no logits, no gradients. Each query yields one bit: classified the way I want, or not? Performance is judged by queries-to-success: how many queries to drive the perturbation norm (here $\ell_2$) below a small target.

Sign-OPT inherits OPT's reformulation wholesale. Stand at the original image $x_0$, shine a beam in direction $\theta$, and let $g(\theta)$ be the distance traveled before the label flips. The goal is the direction whose boundary distance is smallest.

Term by term: $x_0$ is the clean image, $\theta/\lVert\theta\rVert$ the unit beam direction, $\lambda$ the distance, $f$ the label oracle, $y_0$ the original class. $g(\theta)$ is the first distance at which the label becomes wrong; minimizing it over $\theta$ finds the smallest perturbation. Everything novel in Sign-OPT is about estimating the gradient of $g$ more cheaply than OPT did — nothing about the objective itself changes.

pages.title: Why OPT's gradient estimate is wasteful
pages.subtitle: Magnitude is expensive; direction is cheap

blocks.html: Recall how OPT estimates a directional derivative: it computes $g(\theta+\beta u)$ for a random nudge $u$ and compares it to $g(\theta)$. The trouble is that each of those $g$ values is defined by a boundary crossing, so computing it requires a binary search — perhaps 10–20 queries — just to learn a single real number.

Now count the waste. A gradient estimate averages over $Q\approx 20$ random directions; each needs its own binary search of, say, 15 queries; that is ~300 queries for one gradient. And then OPT immediately normalizes the descent step, throwing away almost all of that hard-won magnitude information. You paid for a precise altitude reading and used only its sign.

The key observation that unlocks the whole paper: whether $g$ increased or decreased when you nudged $\theta$ by $u$ can be decided without ever finding the new boundary distance. You do not have to bisect to the new boundary — you only have to check one cleverly chosen point. That collapses ~15 queries per direction down to one.

pages.title: One query tells you the sign
pages.subtitle: The single-query directional test

blocks.html: Here is the trick, with a concrete picture. You already know the current boundary radius $g(\theta)$ along direction $\theta$ — say it is $\lambda = 5.0$. You are at the boundary. Now consider a slightly rotated direction $\theta + \beta u$ and step out to the same radius 5.0 along it. Ask the model one question: is this new point adversarial?

items: If it is already adversarial at radius 5.0, the boundary along $\theta+\beta u$ must be nearer than 5.0 — so $g$ decreased. Sign $= -1$: this rotation helps.
If it is still correctly classified at radius 5.0, the boundary moved farther out — so $g$ increased. Sign $= +1$: this rotation hurts.

blocks.tex: \text{sign}\big(g(\theta + \beta u) - g(\theta)\big) = \begin{cases} -1 & \text{if } f\!\left(x_0 + g(\theta)\,\tfrac{\theta+\beta u}{\lVert\theta+\beta u\rVert}\right) \neq y_0 \\[4pt] +1 & \text{otherwise} \end{cases}

blocks.html: Reading it: probe at the old radius $g(\theta)$ but in the slightly rotated direction $\theta+\beta u$. A single hard-label query returns whether $f$ is wrong (across the boundary → sign $-1$) or still right (sign $+1$). No binary search, no magnitude — just one bit that happens to be exactly the sign we need. This is the entire mechanical heart of the paper.

pages.title: Building a gradient from many signs
pages.subtitle: The Sign-OPT estimator and descent loop

blocks.html: One sign tells you about one direction; to build a full gradient you take a vote. Sample $Q$ random probe directions $u_q$, get each one's sign with a single query, and combine them into an estimated gradient. The only shared cost is one binary search to know $g(\theta)$ for the current $\theta$ — after that, $Q$ directions cost just $Q$ queries total, versus OPT's $Q$ full binary searches.

Term by term: $u_q$ is a random Gaussian probe direction; the $\text{sign}(\cdot)$ is the one-query test from the previous page, returning $\pm 1$; multiplying by $u_q$ casts each direction's vote; averaging over $Q$ of them gives the estimated gradient $\hat{g}$; then $\theta$ takes a descent step with learning rate $\eta$ and is renormalized. Directions that bring the boundary closer pull $\theta$ toward them; directions that push it away repel.

Is this legitimate? It is a biased estimator — discarding magnitude means $\hat{g}$ does not point exactly along the true gradient. But the paper proves it still has positive correlation with the true gradient, so descent converges to a stationary point of $g$. You trade a little directional accuracy for an enormous saving in queries, and the trade pays off handsomely.
Trading exact gradient magnitudes for one-bit sign votes is the whole game: a little bias in the direction, an order-of-magnitude saving in queries.

pages.title: An order of magnitude fewer queries
pages.subtitle: Sign-OPT versus OPT and Boundary Attack

blocks.html: The numbers are decisive. On MNIST, CIFAR-10, and ImageNet, Sign-OPT reaches a target perturbation norm with roughly 5–10× fewer queries than OPT, and dramatically fewer than the original Boundary Attack. At a fixed query budget it also tends to produce a smaller final perturbation than competing methods — the improvement compounds, because cheaper gradient estimates buy more descent steps per dollar of queries.

The authors back this with a convergence analysis for the sign-based estimator, showing that despite using only one bit per probe direction the iteration provably converges to a stationary point of $g$. The method handles both untargeted and targeted attacks (initialize the beam toward a target-class image) and, like OPT, needs nothing but the label oracle — so it also applies to non-differentiable models.

Sign-OPT showed that the query cost of hard-label attacks could be cut by an order of magnitude with a single conceptual move: replace expensive distance estimates with cheap one-bit sign tests. That pushed label-only attacks across an important line — from possible but impractical toward a realistic threat against deployed, paid APIs where every query is metered.

It also crystallized a lesson that recurs across black-box optimization: do not estimate more than the algorithm consumes. Gradient descent with normalization only ever uses the direction, so paying for precise magnitudes is waste. The same sign-only philosophy appears in signSGD and other communication-efficient methods.

In the family tree, Sign-OPT sits directly downstream of OPT (which it accelerates) and alongside HopSkipJump, a contemporaneous line that instead estimates the gradient direction at the boundary via Monte-Carlo sampling and adds geometric step sizing. Together they define the modern frontier of query-efficient hard-label attacks.
Sign-OPT: you only need the sign of the directional derivative, obtainable with one extra query per probe direction — yielding 5–10× fewer queries than OPT for the same attack.
